fixes.explanation: Friends are a nice thought, baker, but the verse says lips. The writer says his inmost being will rejoice when "…your lips speak what is right." Friends can cheer from the sidelines, but the lips in this verse belong to the son.

It's the other way around, baker. The writer says, "For surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off." So the card has it backwards. Just before that, he tells his son to always continue in the fear of the LORD.

That's right, friend. The writer says, "For surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off." The card flips it around. Just before that, he tells his son to always continue in the fear of the LORD.

Poverty, baker. The writer says, "For the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty…" The crowd he warned about in verse 20 is the crowd that poverty is coming for. And he's not done, because drowsiness gets a say too.

Yes, baker. The writer says, "May your father and mother be glad, and may she who gave you birth rejoice!" Verse 24 just before it speaks of a father rejoicing, and here the wish covers both parents. Mom is in it too.

That's right, baker. The writer says, "For a prostitute is a deep pit, and an adulteress is a narrow well." I think this part is heavy, so I'll keep it short. The pictures are a pit that's deep and a well that's narrow.

That's the word, baker. The writer says, "Like a robber she lies in wait and multiplies the faithless among men." She's pictured like a robber lying in wait. What grows in number is the faithless among men.

Wise isn't the word here, friend. The writer says she "…multiplies the faithless among men." She's pictured like a robber lying in wait. What grows in number is the faithless, so that's the word that fits.
Wealthy is a fair guess, baker, but money isn't in this verse. The writer says she "…multiplies the faithless among men." She's pictured like a robber lying in wait. The word is faithless.

Riches would be an interesting answer, friend, but the verse doesn't say it. After the six questions, the writer answers, "Those who linger over wine, who go to taste mixed drinks." Wine is the answer, not a big bank account. Bloodshot eyes are the last of the six questions he asks.

A stone sinking is a strong picture, baker, but it's not the one in the verse. The writer says, "In the end it bites like a snake and stings like a viper." Wine gets a snake that bites and a viper that stings. And he puts it at the end.

Beautiful is how the wine looked in verse 31, baker, red and sparkling. But in verse 33 the writer says the eyes will see "strange things." The full line is, "Your eyes will see strange things, and your mind will utter perversities."

That's what the text says, baker. The drinker asks, "When can I wake up to search for another drink?" I think this one is sad, because he was beaten and didn't know it, and he still asks about another drink. The passage ends on that question.

Going after whoever hit him would make sense, friend, but that's not what he says. He says, "They struck me, but I feel no pain! They beat me, but I did not know it!" Then he asks, "When can I wake up to search for another drink?" The drink is what he asks about.

I'd love to hear that ending, baker, but the drinker doesn't say it. He asks, "When can I wake up to search for another drink?" I think that's the sad part. The only thing he asks about is another drink, not getting out.
